Second-largest branch of [[Islam]], defined by the belief that [[Muhammad]] designated his cousin and son-in-law [[Ali|Ali ibn Abi Talib]] (r. 656–661) as his successor.

Shia Muslims hold that Ali was the rightful political successor (caliph) and the divinely guided spiritual leader (imam) of the Muslim community. They maintain that his right was unjustly usurped at the meeting of Saqifa, where [[Abu Bakr]] (r. 632–634) was chosen as caliph. Sunni Muslims accept Abu Bakr, [[Umar]] (r. 634–644), and [[Uthman]] (r. 644–656). Shia Muslims cite Muhammad's sermon at Ghadir Khumm as a clear designation of Ali; Sunni scholars tend to read it as a general affirmation of his merit. The Shia emerged as a distinct movement during the First Fitna (656–661). Scholars debate their origins: some Western historians describe early Shia Islam as merely a political faction, while others call that view anachronistic.

Shia Muslims believe the imamate continued through Ali's sons, Hasan and Husayn, after whom various branches emerged. Central to Shia devotion is reverence for the ahl al-bayt, the family of Muhammad, regarded as infallible inheritors of his knowledge and spiritual authority. Holy sites include the shrines of Ali in Najaf and Husayn in Karbala; mourning rituals commemorate Husayn's death in 680. The principal branches are Twelverism, Isma'ilism, and Zaydism. Twelvers, estimated at 85–90% of Shia Muslims, hold that twelve imams succeeded Ali. The [[Fatimid Caliphate]] (909–1171) was a Shia state.

Shia Muslims are estimated at 10–13% of the world's Muslims, roughly 200–260 million. They form a majority in [[Iran]], Iraq, and Azerbaijan and almost half the Muslim population of Lebanon and Bahrain. Iran is the only country where Shia Islam officially underlies both the legal framework and the system of governance.

Religion of [[Japan]] centered on the veneration of kami, supernatural entities believed to inhabit all things.

Shinto is often regarded by its practitioners as Japan's indigenous religion and as a nature religion. It has no central authority, single creator, or specific doctrine. The kami are worshipped at household shrines (kamidana) and public shrines (jinja). Priests called kannushi staff the public shrines and oversee offerings to the kami, intended to cultivate harmony and solicit blessing. Other rituals include kagura dances, rites of passage, and kami festivals; shrines also offer [[Divination|divination]]. Purity, pursued through ritual washing, is a major concern. Little emphasis falls on moral codes or afterlife beliefs, although the dead can become kami.

Historians debate when Shinto became a distinct religion. Kami veneration has been traced to Japan's Yayoi period (300 BC–AD 250). [[Buddhism]] entered Japan at the end of the Kofun period and spread rapidly; the two became functionally inseparable in a process called shinbutsu-shūgō. Kami worship was first recorded in the 8th-century [[Kojiki]] and *Nihon Shoki*.During the Meiji era (1868–1912), nationalist leaders expelled Buddhist influence and formed State Shinto, which some historians regard as the origin of Shinto as a distinct religion; citizens were encouraged to worship the emperor as a kami, though the emperor's descent from [[Amaterasu]] was a longstanding tradition. Shinto spread to other parts of East Asia with the [[Empire of Japan]]. After Japan's defeat in [[World War II|World War II]], it was formally separated from the state.

Shinto is numerically Japan's largest religion, with Buddhism second. Most Japanese take part in both Shinto and Buddhist activities, and aspects of Shinto appear in various [[New religious movement|new religious movements]].

Large watercraft designed for travel across the surface of a body of water, carrying cargo or passengers, or supporting specialized tasks such as warfare, oceanography, and fishing.

Ships are generally distinguished from [[Boat|boats]] by size, shape, load capacity, and purpose, but there is no universally accepted distinction. A common notion holds that a ship can carry a boat but not the reverse. Some large vessels are traditionally called boats, notably [[Submarine|submarines]]. The word has meant either simply a large vessel or, from the mid-18th century, specifically a full-rigged ship with three or more masts, all square-rigged.

The earliest historical evidence of boats is found in Egypt in the 4th millennium BC. Model ships from [[Mesopotamia]] date to the same period. The [[Austronesian peoples]], who originated in what is now [[Taiwan]], used catamarans, outriggers, and crab claw sails to colonize Pacific islands and [[Madagascar]]. For most of history, transport by ship was cheaper, safer, and faster than overland travel, a principle changed only by railways in the mid-19th century and commercial aviation in the second half of the 20th. Rome consumed about 150,000 tons of Egyptian grain a year in the first three centuries AD, delivered by sailing and oared ships.

Ship transport carries the largest portion of world commerce. In 2024, ships had a global cargo capacity of 2.4 billion tons; the three largest classes were dry bulk carriers (43%), [[Tanker (ship)|oil tankers]] (28%), and container ships (14%).

Brief work of narrative fiction in [[Prose|prose]] that can typically be read in a single sitting.

A short story focuses on a self-contained incident or a series of linked incidents, intended to evoke a single effect or mood. It uses the techniques of the [[Novel|novel]], but typically to a lesser degree. Defining it is problematic. [[Edgar Allan Poe]]'s essay "The Philosophy of Composition" (1846) made the classic point that it should be readable in one sitting, and H. G. Wells said it should take from fifteen to fifty minutes to read aloud. Somerset Maugham held that a story must have a plot, while [[Anton Chekhov]] thought it should be a suggestive "slice of life" with neither beginning nor end. [[William Faulkner]] called it character-driven. Typical length is 1,000 to 4,000 words, with some up to 15,000; under 1,000 is flash fiction.

The form descends from oral storytelling traditions that produced epics such as the *Ramayana*, the *Mahabharata*, and Homer's *Iliad* and *Odyssey*, and it existed as legends, myths, and fables in ancient communities. The anecdote, a brief realistic narrative embodying a point, was popular during the [[Roman Empire]]; many were collected in the 13th or 14th century as the *Gesta Romanorum*. In Europe, written form developed in the early 14th century, most notably with [[Giovanni Boccaccio]]'s *Decameron* and [[Geoffrey Chaucer]]'s *Canterbury Tales*.

The modern short story developed in the early 19th century, and the term acquired its modern meaning in the 1880s, having initially referred to children's tales. Washington Irving, Nathaniel Hawthorne, Nikolai Gogol, and Guy de Maupassant shaped it, and the 20th century brought expansive experimentation. Its form has been closely tied to the publishing industry.

Austrian neurologist, founder of [[Psychoanalysis]].

Born Sigismund Schlomo Freud in Freiberg, Moravia (now Příbor, Czech Republic), he grew up in [[Vienna]] after his family moved there in 1860. He entered the [[University of Vienna]] in 1873 and graduated with an MD in 1881. His early research on nervous tissue, in Ernst Brücke's physiology laboratory, proved seminal for the discovery of the [[Neuron|neuron]] in the 1890s.

Psychoanalysis is a clinical method for treating pathologies arising from conflicts in the psyche through dialogue between patient and analyst. Freud introduced free association, the interpretation of dreams, and the analysis of transference. His redefinition of sexuality to include infantile stages led him to formulate the [[Oedipus complex]] as a central tenet. He analyzed dreams as wish fulfillments, which gave him models for understanding symptom formation and repression, and on this basis he elaborated a theory of the unconscious and a model of psychic structure comprising id, ego, and superego. He postulated libido, a sexualized psychic energy, and a death drive, the source of compulsion, aggression, and neurotic guilt. His later work offered a wide-ranging interpretation and critique of religion and culture. He emigrated to London in 1938 amid Nazi persecution.

Though less prevalent in diagnostic and clinical practice, psychoanalysis remains influential in [[Psychology|psychology]], [[Psychiatry|psychiatry]], and the [[Humanities|humanities]]. It continues to generate debate over its therapeutic efficacy, its scientific status, and whether it advances or hinders the feminist cause. Critics, including philosophers of science, call key elements pseudoscientific for relying on case studies rather than controlled evidence. W. H. Auden's 1940 tribute described Freud as "no more a person now but a whole climate of opinion / under whom we conduct our different lives".

Monotheistic Indian religion and philosophy that originated in the [[Punjab]] region around the end of the 15th century.

Followed by 25–30 million adherents, known as Sikhs, it is one of the most recently founded major religions. It developed from the teachings of [[Guru Nanak]], the first guru, and nine successors. The tenth, [[Guru Gobind Singh]], named the [[Guru Granth Sahib]] as his successor, closing the line of human gurus; Sikhs regard it as the 11th and eternally living guru.

Core beliefs, articulated in the Guru Granth Sahib, include faith in one creator (Ik Onkar), called Waheguru; the divine unity and equality of all humankind; selfless service (sevā); striving for justice for all (sarbat da bhala); and honest conduct and livelihood. It rejects claims that any one tradition has a monopoly on absolute truth, so Sikhs do not actively proselytise, though voluntary converts are generally accepted. [[Meditation]] and remembrance of God (simran) are expressed through devotional music (kirtan) or inwardly through naam japna. Ego, anger, greed, attachment, and lust, the "Five Thieves", are held to distract from devotion.

The religion developed in times of religious persecution and gained converts from both [[Hinduism]] and [[Islam]]. The Mughal emperors executed two gurus, Guru Arjan and Guru Tegh Bahadur, after they refused to convert to Islam. In response, Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa in 1699, an order to protect freedom of conscience and religion whose members embody the ideal of the sant-sipāhī ("saint-soldier"). Baptised Sikhs wear the five Ks, articles of faith that include kesh (uncut hair), which is why most religious Sikh men wear a turban. Some Sikhs prefer the term Sikhi to Sikhism.

[[Chemical element]] (symbol Si, atomic number 14), a hard, brittle crystalline solid with a blue-grey metallic lustre.

A tetravalent non-metal (sometimes considered a metalloid) and [[Semiconductor|semiconductor]], silicon belongs to group 14 of the periodic table, below carbon, and is relatively unreactive. It melts at 1414 °C and boils at 3265 °C, the second highest values among the metalloids and nonmetals after boron. Its density is 2.329 g/cm³, and its main stable isotope is ²⁸Si (92.2%). It is the eighth most common element in the universe by mass and, at about 28% by mass, the second most abundant in the Earth's crust after [[Oxygen|oxygen]]. It rarely occurs pure; more than 90% of the crust is composed of [[Silicate|silicate]] minerals.

Its high affinity for oxygen long delayed isolation. Antoine Lavoisier suspected in 1787 that silica was an oxide of an unknown element. Humphry Davy proposed the name "silicium", from Latin *silex*, "flint"; in 1817 Thomas Thomson gave it its present name. [[Jöns Jacob Berzelius]] is usually credited with the discovery for preparing and purifying amorphous silicon.

Most silicon is used commercially without being separated, as clay, silica sand, and stone in construction, in Portland cement and [[Concrete|concrete]], and in porcelain and glass. Silicon carbide serves as an abrasive and in high-strength ceramics, and silicon is the basis of the synthetic polymers called [[Silicone|silicones]]. Less than 15% of silicon is highly purified for semiconductor electronics, where it is essential to transistors, solar cells, and [[Integrated circuit|integrated circuit]] chips, so the late 20th and early 21st centuries have been called the Silicon Age. Sea sponges, diatoms, and radiolaria build skeletons of silica.

Network of [[Asia|Asian]] trade routes, active from the second century BC until the mid-15th century, linking East and West.

Spanning over 6,400 km on land, it facilitated economic, cultural, political, and religious exchange. It took its name from the trade in silk textiles produced mainly in China; the term was coined in the late 19th century and popularized in 1877 by Ferdinand von Richthofen. The network began with the expansion of the [[Han dynasty]] into Central Asia around 114 BC, through the missions of the imperial envoy [[Zhang Qian]]. The [[Parthian Empire]] bridged the network to the Mediterranean, and by the first century AD Chinese silk was widely sought in Rome, Egypt, and Greece. Eastern goods included tea, dyes, perfumes, and porcelain; Western exports included horses, camels, honey, wine, and gold.

The network was decentralized and security sparse; few travelers covered its full length, relying instead on middlemen such as the Sogdians. It also carried religious and scientific ideas, especially those of [[Buddhism]], and plague, possibly contributing to the [[Black Death]]. From 1453 the [[Ottoman Empire]] competed for control of the overland routes, which prompted European polities to seek alternatives and began the Age of Discovery. "New Silk Road" now describes infrastructure projects such as the Chinese [[Belt and Road Initiative]]. UNESCO designated the Chang'an-Tianshan corridor a World Heritage Site in 2014.

The concept is contested. Some historians prefer "Silk Routes" because it was never a single route. Warwick Ball calls it a "myth" of modern academia, arguing that the maritime spice trade mattered more to the Roman economy and that no free overland movement of goods existed before the Mongol Empire. Critics add that the term sidelines steppe nomads, India, and Iran.

[[Chemical element]] (symbol Ag, from Latin *argentum*; atomic number 47), a soft, white, lustrous transition metal.

Silver has the highest electrical conductivity, thermal conductivity, and reflectivity of any metal. It is extremely ductile and malleable, with a density of 10.503 g/cm³, a melting point of 961.8 °C, and a boiling point of 2,162 °C. It resists oxidation in air but tarnishes on exposure to sulfur compounds, forming black silver sulfide. It resembles its group 11 neighbours, [[Copper|copper]] and [[Gold|gold]]. Natural silver consists of two stable isotopes, ¹⁰⁷Ag (51.839%) and ¹⁰⁹Ag.

Silver occurs as native silver, as an alloy with gold ([[Electrum|electrum]]), and in minerals such as acanthite, argentite, and chlorargyrite. Most is recovered as a byproduct of lead–zinc, copper, and gold mining. World mine production was about 25,300 metric tons in 2024, led by Mexico (6,300 tons), China (3,300 tons), Peru (3,100 tons), and Poland (1,300 tons).

One of the seven metals of antiquity, silver has long been valued as a precious metal and a coinage metal, with an enduring role in monetary systems, jewellery, tableware, and decorative arts. Its purity is measured per mille; a 94%-pure alloy is "0.940 fine". Because pure silver is soft, [[Coin|coinage]] and jewellery silver is usually alloyed with copper.

Industrial uses accounted for about 59% of demand in 2024. They include photovoltaics, electrical contacts, brazing alloys, catalysis, mirrors, and antimicrobial materials. Silver halides are important in photographic film and paper, though digital imaging has reduced demand. Silver is rarely used for its conductivity because of its cost, but during World War II in the U.S., 13,540 tons were used for the electromagnets of calutrons that enriched uranium, because of a wartime shortage of copper.

Venezuelan military officer and statesman who led much of northern and western South America to independence from the [[Spanish Empire]].

Known as El Libertador, "the Liberator", he was born in [[Caracas]] into a wealthy criollo family but lost both parents as a child. Living in [[Madrid]] from 1800 to 1802, he was introduced to Enlightenment philosophy and married María Teresa Rodríguez del Toro y Alaysa, who died of yellow fever in 1803. On a Grand Tour that ended in [[Rome]] in 1805, he swore to end Spanish rule. He returned to Venezuela in 1807.

Bolívar began his military career in 1810 as a militia officer in the Venezuelan War of Independence. After Spanish forces subdued New Granada in 1815, he went into exile on [[Jamaica]]. In [[Haiti]], he befriended the revolutionary leader Alexandre Pétion, and after promising to abolish slavery he received military support and returned to Venezuela. He established a third republic in 1817 and in 1819 crossed the [[Andes]] to liberate New Granada. His forces and allies defeated the Spanish in Venezuela and Panama in 1821, Ecuador in 1822, Peru in 1824, and Bolivia in 1825. Venezuela, New Granada, Ecuador, and Panama were merged into the Republic of Colombia ([[Gran Colombia]]), with Bolívar as president there and in Peru and Bolivia.

 He pursued republican government but favored strong centralized authority, including a president-for-life in some constitutional provisions. His insistence on unitary governance over federalism provoked rebellions from autonomists such as José Antonio Páez. Disillusioned, he resigned the presidency of Colombia and died of tuberculosis in 1830; Gran Colombia dissolved by 1831. He is regarded throughout Latin America as a national icon; Bolivia and Venezuela are named after him.
